explanation_text: On a soroban (Japanese abacus), each vertical rod holds beads whose place—ones, tens, hundreds—gives them their value, just as a digit's position determines how much it is worth. An upper bead counts as 5 and each lower bead as 1, but only the column tells you the true magnitude.
image_prompt: Illustrate a soroban with its vertical rods labeled ones, tens, and hundreds, showing how a bead's position determines its value.

explanation_text: Packing a bento box is addition: each onigiri or tamagoyaki slice you add increases the total. Eating a piece is subtraction: taking food away lowers the amount left in the box.
image_prompt: Show a bento box being filled with onigiri pieces one by one, then one being removed, with totals shown changing.

explanation_text: Sushi chefs arrange nigiri in identical rows on a platter; 4 rows of 5 pieces gives 20 pieces—that is multiplication. Sharing those 20 pieces among 4 guests gives 5 each—that is division.
image_prompt: Display a sushi platter with nigiri laid out in equal rows, showing 4 rows of 5, then pieces split evenly among diners.

explanation_text: At the genkan (entryway), slippers are stored in pairs. When every slipper has a partner, the count is even; a single lone slipper left behind makes the total odd.
image_prompt: Show slippers lined up in pairs at a Japanese entryway, with one single slipper at the end to represent an odd number.

explanation_text: Walking the tunnel of torii gates at Fushimi Inari, pilgrims often count every second or every fifth gate—a rhythmic jump through the numbers that mirrors skip counting and number patterns.
image_prompt: Show a path lined with torii gates, with every fifth gate highlighted to illustrate skip counting by 5s.

japanese_culture: Koi fish sizes in a pond
explanation_text: Koi in a garden pond come in different lengths. Holding two beside each other shows which is longer or shorter—the same greater-than and less-than thinking used to compare numbers.
image_prompt: Show two koi fish of different lengths in a pond, with > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: A cook making onigiri estimates how much cooked rice is needed—'about one full bowl for three'—rather than measuring every grain. This rough-but-handy thinking is exactly like rounding to a convenient number.
image_prompt: Show a cook scooping rice for onigiri with a rice bowl, labeling approximate amounts such as 'about 2 cups'.

explanation_text: A round mochi cake is cut into 4 or 8 equal pieces for a celebration. Each equal slice is a fraction of the whole cake—1/4 or 1/8—with the cut lines showing exactly how the whole is shared.
image_prompt: Show a round mochi cake cut into equal wedges, each piece labeled with its fraction such as 1/4.

explanation_text: Cutting a mochi cake into 2 halves and then each half into 2 more gives 4 quarters. One half of the cake and two quarters are the same amount—equal fractions with different names.
image_prompt: Show one mochi cake cut into halves and another into quarters, linking 1/2 to 2/4 as equal amounts.

explanation_text: If 4 onigiri are shared by 8 guests, each guest takes 4/8 of the whole. Since 4 of the 8 pieces is the same as half the batch, the fraction simplifies to 1/2—the same share, written more simply.
image_prompt: Show a tray of onigiri where 4 of 8 pieces are grouped and labeled 4/8 = 1/2.

explanation_text: At a tea ceremony, 3 full teapots and 1 half-full pot together hold 3½ pots of tea. The whole pots plus the fraction make a mixed number.
image_prompt: Show three full teapots and one half-full teapot labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: When cooked rice fills more than one bowl but is still counted in bowl-sized parts, you have more than a whole—for example 5/3 bowls. This top-heavy value is an improper fraction, as common as a heaping bowl of rice at dinnertime.
image_prompt: Show several rice bowls where the rice totals more than one full bowl, labeled with a fraction greater than 1.

explanation_text: Pouring a half-cup of miso broth from one bowl into another with a quarter-cup gives three-quarters of a cup. Combining smaller fractional portions into a total is fraction addition.
image_prompt: Show small bowls of miso broth being combined into one bowl, with the pieces labeled as fractions adding together.

explanation_text: A full cup of sencha holds a whole portion. After drinking a quarter of it, three-quarters remain. Removing a fractional part from a whole is fraction subtraction.
image_prompt: Show a cup of green tea with one-quarter poured away, the remaining three-quarters labeled.

japanese_culture: Half of a half nori sheet
explanation_text: Folding a nori sheet in half and then taking half of that folded half gives a quarter of the original sheet. Finding a part of a part is fraction multiplication: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
image_prompt: Show a nori sheet folded in half, then half of the half marked off and labeled 1/4.

japanese_culture: Cutting a maki roll into halves
explanation_text: A maki sushi roll is one whole. Cutting it into half-roll pieces asks how many halves fit inside: 1 ÷ 1/2 = 2. Dividing by a fraction counts how many of the smaller pieces make the whole.
image_prompt: Show a maki roll cut into half pieces, illustrating how two halves make one whole roll.

explanation_text: Japanese rice cookers measure water in liters and milliliters. Adding 0.5 liter to 1 liter gives 1.5 liters—a decimal that separates whole liters from tenths with a decimal point.
image_prompt: Show a measuring cup for rice water marked at 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 liters.

explanation_text: Half a liter of water for a rice cooker and 0.5 liters are the same amount written two ways. Moving between 1/2 and 0.5 is converting a fraction to a decimal.
image_prompt: Show a water measuring cup marked both ½ and 0.5 at the same level.

explanation_text: Japanese students take tests scored out of 100. Answering 90 of 100 questions correctly means 90 out of every 100, or 90%—a percent is just a fraction with denominator 100.
image_prompt: Show a Japanese school test paper with 90/100 correct and a large 90% mark beside it.

explanation_text: Japan's consumption tax is 10%, so a 2,000-yen item costs 200 yen in tax. Finding 10% of the price shows how a percent extracts a part of a number.
image_prompt: Show a store price tag of ¥2,000 with a 10% consumption tax note adding ¥200.

explanation_text: If the tea ceremony host doesn't know how many guests will arrive, the cups needed are an unknown amount—written as x. A variable is just a number whose value is not yet known.
image_prompt: Show a stack of teacups with a question mark, beside an x symbol representing the unknown count.

explanation_text: If a tray already holds 3 teacups and x more guests are expected, the total is expressed as 3 + x. Combining known numbers with variables gives an expression.
image_prompt: Show a tea tray with three cups next to an empty space marked x, written as 3 + x.

explanation_text: A tenbin (traditional balance scale) tips only when the two pans hold different weights. When both sides hold equal amounts, the scale balances—exactly what an equation states: two sides that are equal.
image_prompt: Show a traditional balance scale with equal weights on both pans, labeled as a balanced equation.

explanation_text: A vendor carrying buckets on a tenbinbo (shoulder pole) keeps it level by adding or removing weight from one side. Undoing one change to restore balance is like solving a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a carrying pole with a bucket on one side being adjusted to match the other, symbolizing a one-step balance.

explanation_text: Making matcha takes fixed steps: scoop the powder, add hot water, then whisk with a chasen. Two operations in the right sequence, just like solving a two-step equation by undoing steps in reverse order.
image_prompt: Show the matcha sequence—scooping powder, adding water, whisking—to represent ordered, step-by-step solving.

explanation_text: A five-tier pagoda (gojunotō) has a bottom tier taller than the top tier. Comparing two tiers uses the same 'greater than' and 'less than' language as inequalities.
image_prompt: Show a pagoda with its tiers compared using > and < symbols between different levels.

explanation_text: The tea ceremony (chanoyu) follows a strict order—purify the utensils, whisk the tea, then serve. Doing steps out of order ruins the result, just as operations in a math expression must follow a set sequence.
image_prompt: Show a numbered sequence of tea ceremony steps, each labeled with math operations in parentheses.

explanation_text: When a shoji's washi paper panel tears, a fresh panel of the same size is installed in its place. Swapping an equal replacement for a broken part is like substituting a value into a variable.
image_prompt: Show a shoji screen with one torn panel being replaced by an identical new panel, representing substitution.

explanation_text: On Tanabata, Vega and Altair shine as two bright points among the stars. Each star marks a single location in the sky, just as a point marks a single position in geometry.
image_prompt: Show a Tanabata night sky with individual stars marked as points on a faint coordinate grid.

explanation_text: Every fold in origami leaves a long, straight crease that runs edge to edge, like a geometric line that extends in both directions through the paper.
image_prompt: Show a sheet of origami paper with straight fold creases drawn across it, representing lines.

explanation_text: A sensu (folding fan) opens from a small sliver to a wide sweep. The space between its two edge ribs is an angle, and the more it opens, the larger the angle grows.
image_prompt: Show a folding fan partially open, with the angle between its ribs clearly marked and labeled.

explanation_text: The wooden lattice of a shoji screen has vertical and horizontal bars that meet at perfect right angles, forming a strong grid—lines meeting at 90° are perpendicular.
image_prompt: Show the wooden lattice of a shoji screen with crossbars marked at 90° angles.

explanation_text: The two rails of a shinkansen track run side by side at a constant distance apart and never meet. Lines that stay equally spaced forever are parallel.
image_prompt: Show shinkansen railway tracks running side by side into the distance, never crossing.

explanation_text: Kumiko woodwork joins thin slats into closed shapes—triangles, diamonds, and hexagons—that repeat across a panel. Each closed, many-sided shape is a polygon.
image_prompt: Show a kumiko wooden lattice panel made of repeating triangular and diamond shapes.

explanation_text: The first folds of an origami crane create sharp triangles: fold a square corner to corner and you get a right isosceles triangle. Triangles are the building blocks of countless origami designs.
image_prompt: Show an origami square folded corner to corner, revealing a triangle shape.

explanation_text: Tatami mats are rectangles with four sides and four right angles. Japanese rooms are measured by how many mats they hold, and every mat is a quadrilateral.
image_prompt: Show a tatami room floor with rectangular mats labeled as quadrilaterals.

explanation_text: Strolling the stone edge of a koi pond and measuring the full distance around it gives the perimeter—the total length of a shape's boundary.
image_prompt: Show a koi pond with a dashed line tracing its full edge, labeled as the perimeter.

explanation_text: Japanese rooms are sized in jo, the number of tatami mats that cover the floor. Counting how many mats fit inside a room measures its area—the space the floor covers.
image_prompt: Show a room floor covered in tatami mats, counted and shaded to show its area.

explanation_text: A wooden ofuro (Japanese bath) holds a fixed amount of hot water. That capacity—how much the tub can contain—is its volume.
image_prompt: Show a wooden Japanese bath filled with water, with the capacity labeled in liters.

explanation_text: Japanese manhole covers are famously round, some decorated like art. Measuring one shows the radius (center to edge), the diameter (edge to edge through the center), and the circumference (the rim all around).
image_prompt: Show a round Japanese manhole cover labeled with radius, diameter, and circumference lines.

explanation_text: Wrap a measuring tape around a manhole cover and compare it to the width across: the rim is always about 3.14 times the diameter, no matter the size. That constant ratio is π.
image_prompt: Show a manhole cover with circumference and diameter measured, labeled as C = πd.

explanation_text: Kyoto's streets run in tidy rows and columns, with each crossing where an east-west road meets a north-south one. Just as on a coordinate plane, every intersection can be named by a row and column.
image_prompt: Show a map of Kyoto's grid streets with x and y axes overlaid.

japanese_culture: Marking torii gates on a shrine map
explanation_text: Plotting each torii gate's location on a map of a shrine path places a point at a specific spot, exactly as you plot a point at coordinates (x, y) on a graph.
image_prompt: Show a shrine map with torii gates marked as points at labeled coordinates.

explanation_text: Kimono designs often mirror across the center back seam: the left and right halves are reflections of each other. Splitting a pattern into balanced mirror halves is symmetry.
image_prompt: Show a kimono with a mirrored pattern divided by a central vertical line.

explanation_text: Folding origami is a series of transformations: paper is reflected along crease lines, rotated to new positions, and translated across the work surface to build the final shape.
image_prompt: Show origami paper mid-folding, with arrows showing reflection, rotation, and sliding moves.

explanation_text: A matcha recipe calls for a fixed ratio, like 1 part powder to 2 parts hot water. Keeping that proportion from one bowl to the next is using a ratio.
image_prompt: Show a matcha bowl beside a chasen, with powder and water labeled in a 1:2 ratio.

explanation_text: When a kimono pattern is printed larger for a banner, every curve and gap grows by the same factor so the design still looks identical—maintaining proportion keeps the ratios the same.
image_prompt: Show a small kimono pattern and a larger copy of the same design, linked by a scaling arrow.

explanation_text: A shinkansen traveling 300 kilometers in 1 hour moves at a unit rate of 300 km per hour—an amount expressed for a single unit of time.
image_prompt: Show a shinkansen train with a speed readout of 300 km per hour.

explanation_text: A visitor's map shrinks a large temple garden into a small sheet while keeping every path and pond in the same relative position and size—a scale drawing.
image_prompt: Show a temple garden beside a smaller scaled map with a legend reading '1 cm = 5 m'.

explanation_text: When a shrine's daily visitors rise from 100 to 120, the number grows by 20 of the original 100—a 20% increase. Comparing a new amount to the original as a percent is percent change.
image_prompt: Show a shrine entrance with visitor counts rising from 100 to 120, labeled +20%.

explanation_text: At Gion matsuri, organizers tally how many people watch each float pass by, recording the numbers on a clipboard. Gathering and recording counts like these is data collection.
image_prompt: Show a festival recorder tallying visitors on a clipboard during a Gion matsuri parade.

explanation_text: Recording monthly rainfall in Kyoto on a bar graph turns raw numbers into a picture, making it easy to see that the rainy season brings a spike in June.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph of monthly rainfall in Kyoto, with June highlighted.

explanation_text: If a shrine counts 100, 150, and 110 visitors over three days, adding them (360) and dividing by 3 gives 120—the mean, or average, number of visitors per day.
image_prompt: Show a table of daily shrine visitors with the average value highlighted.

explanation_text: Line up tea sets by price, from cheapest to most expensive. The price exactly in the middle of the line is the median.
image_prompt: Show tea sets arranged by price with the middle one highlighted as the median.

explanation_text: In a pond with many koi, if most are orange-white kohaku, that color is the most frequent value in the collection—the mode.
image_prompt: Show a pond of koi in several colors with the orange-white kohaku being the most numerous.

explanation_text: A row of bonsai ranges from the tallest to the shortest tree. The difference between the tallest and shortest heights is the range of the collection.
image_prompt: Show bonsai trees of different heights with the tallest and shortest marked, labeled as the range.

explanation_text: A bar graph can compare how much each Gion matsuri food stall sold, with one bar per stall so the tallest bar shows the busiest seller at a glance.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph of festival food stalls with bars of different heights.

explanation_text: Tracking how many cherry blossoms open each day of April with a connected line shows the bloom climbing, peaking, and fading—a trend only a line graph makes obvious.
image_prompt: Show a line graph of cherry blossom blooms rising and falling across the days of April.

explanation_text: A platter of assorted sushi can be shown as a pie chart, where each slice represents the share of salmon, tuna, or tamago nigiri in the whole assortment.
image_prompt: Show a sushi platter alongside a pie chart dividing the pieces by type with percentages.

explanation_text: In hanafuda, each month has its own flower suit. Reaching into a full deck, the chance of drawing a card from a chosen month is 1 out of 12 suits—a probability.
image_prompt: Show a hanafuda deck with cards laid out by month, one card being drawn with a 1/12 chance label.

explanation_text: The seigaiha pattern layers identical semicircular waves in repeating rows across fabric and ceramics. A motif that repeats itself in order is a pattern.
image_prompt: Show a seigaiha wave pattern with repeating arcs and a highlighted unit that repeats.

explanation_text: On a shinkansen, each travel time maps to exactly one distance traveled: 1 hour gives 300 km, 2 hours give 600 km. Any rule that gives every input one output is a function.
image_prompt: Show a shinkansen with travel time mapping arrows to distance, labeled input to output.
